intro: Match each 'before' condition to what came after it.

left.label: Before 1676: servitude law treated cases individually, no fixed racial rule (1640-1669)
Before 1676: poor white servants and enslaved Africans lived and labored under similar hard conditions
Before 1676: no single event had shown elites what a servant-and-enslaved alliance could do
Before 1754: the thirteen colonies acted separately, with no shared political structure

right.label: After: colonial assemblies write law that splits servitude sharply along racial lines
After: elites move to separate the two groups legally and socially, using race
After: Bacon's Rebellion becomes the proof elites point to from here forward
After: Franklin's Join or Die cartoon (Document 16) becomes the first prominent call to unite against a shared threat

rationale.a: The pre-1676 pattern (Document 13) treats offenses case by case; after Bacon's Rebellion, the law itself splits along racial lines.
rationale.b: Similar conditions before 1676 give way, after, to a deliberate legal and social separation of poor whites from enslaved people.
rationale.c: Bacon's Rebellion is the single event elites point back to when justifying the harder line that follows.
rationale.d: Before 1754 the colonies had no shared political structure; Join or Die (Document 16) is the first prominent argument for uniting them.
